source_text: Klagel. Jerem. 1, 20. Ἐν μὲν οὖν τῇ προφητείᾳ ἀλγεῖ τὴν ψυχὴν ὡς πεισόμενος δει- νότατα· ἐν δὲ τῷ παρόντι Θρήνῳ, ὡς ἤδη τούτων συμβεβηκότων, ἄχθεταί τε καὶ δι' ἁμαρτίας ὁμολογεῖ τὴν χρηστότητα τοῦ θεοῦ πικροτάτην ἑαυτὴν καταστῆσαι, ὡς καὶ ἀτεκνωθῆναι τὴν πολύ- τεκνον, καὶ τὸ δεινότατον, πολεμίᾳ χειρί. προσωποποιίας δὲ οὔσης, οὐ δεῖ ζητεῖν πόλεως κοιλίαν τεκοῦσαν καὶ καρδίαν λελυμένην.
pass_a_gloss: In the prophecy, then, he grieves in soul as one about to suffer most terrible things; but in the present Lament, as these things having already befallen, he is weighed down and through sins confesses that the kindness of God has set herself most bitter—so as even for the many-childed to be made childless, and the most terrible thing, by a hostile hand. And there being a prosōpopoiia / personification, one must not seek a city’s womb that has given birth and a heart that has been loosed.
pass_b_english: In the prophecy, then, he grieves in soul as one about to suffer most terrible things; but in the present Lament, as these things having already befallen, he is weighed down and through sins confesses that the kindness of God has set herself most bitter—so as even for the many-childed to be made childless, and the most terrible thing, by a hostile hand. And there being a personification, one must not seek a city’s womb that has given birth and a heart that has been loosed (Lamentations 1:20).

choices.why: Origen’s Lam 1:22 turns on punitive-yet-healing divine visitation.

anf_compare.notes: No public-domain English of Origen’s Greek Lamentations fragments. Sense checked against Klostermann GCS III. Modern English not copied. OET = no previous English translation.
